definition: The Python exception raised when a connection attempt is answered with RST, usually because nothing is listening on the port.
example: socket.create_connection(("localhost", 9)) raises ConnectionRefusedError if no service runs there.

definition: The Python exception raised when the peer aborts an established connection with RST.
example: Reading from a socket whose peer crashed and rebooted can raise ConnectionResetError.

definition: The Python exception raised when writing to a connection that can no longer send, for example after the peer has reset it.
example: Writing to a socket after the peer reset the connection can raise BrokenPipeError.

definition: The Python exception raised when a socket operation exceeds the timeout set with settimeout(); socket.timeout is an older name for it.
example: With conn.settimeout(5), a recv() that waits more than 5 seconds raises TimeoutError.

definition: A Python exception meaning input ended unexpectedly. The lesson's recv_exact raises it when the peer closes in the middle of a message.
example: If the peer closes after 2 bytes of a 4-byte header, recv_exact raises EOFError.

definition: Global interpreter lock: a lock in the standard CPython interpreter that lets only one thread run Python code at a time; it is released during blocking I/O such as socket reads.
example: Two CPython threads blocked in recv() do not hold the GIL, so other threads can run.

definition: The standard, reference implementation of Python, written in C; it is what 'python' usually means.
example: python3 on most systems is CPython.

definition: A widely used web server and reverse proxy that serves many connections from a few worker processes using event loops.
example: Nginx with 8 workers can use SO_REUSEPORT so each worker has its own listener.

definition: A background thread that does not keep a Python program alive: when the main thread exits, daemon threads are stopped.
example: threading.Thread(target=handle, daemon=True) creates a daemon thread per connection.

definition: A scheme that makes a client solve a costly puzzle before a server spends resources on it. TCP has no such mechanism; SYN cookies need no client changes.
example: A proof-of-work puzzle might require finding a hash with 20 leading zero bits.

definition: A command-line tool for making HTTP and other network requests, often used to test servers.
example: curl -v https://example.com shows the connection setup and response headers.

definition: Handing work such as checksums or splitting large buffers into segments to the network card or a lower layer, to save CPU.
example: With segmentation offload, the kernel passes a 64 KB buffer to the NIC, which cuts it into 1,460-byte segments.

definition: The smallest unit of data, a single 0 or 1. Network speeds are quoted in bits per second; eight bits make one byte.
example: A 1,500-byte packet is 12,000 bits.

definition: Kilobits per second: thousands of bits per second.
example: 32 kbit/s is 32,000 bits per second.

definition: Kibibyte: exactly 1,024 bytes (2^10).
example: 256 KiB = 262,144 bytes.

definition: Megabyte: a million bytes (10^6). MB/s means megabytes per second; multiply by 8 for Mbit/s.
example: 12.5 MB is 100 megabits.

definition: Mebibyte: exactly 1,048,576 bytes (2^20).
One millionth of a second (µs).
example: RFC 9293 discusses an ISN clock that ticks about every 4 µs.

definition: Sending data again because it seems to have been lost. TCP resends the same bytes with their original sequence numbers, triggered by duplicate ACKs, SACK or RACK evidence, or the retransmission timer.
example: When segment 1001 is lost, the sender retransmits bytes 1001 to 2000 after three duplicate ACKs.

definition: A transfer small enough that round trips (handshakes and slow-start flights), not link bandwidth, decide how long it takes.
example: A 100,000-byte response over a new HTTPS connection at 100 ms RTT takes about five round trips, roughly 500 ms, on almost any link speed.

definition: Proving with cryptography (for example TLS certificates) who the other end of a connection really is. TCP's handshake does not do this: it only shows the peer can receive packets at its address.
example: TLS authenticates a web server with its certificate; the TCP handshake beneath it does not.

definition: The information an endpoint (or a stateful middlebox) keeps about each connection. A TCP endpoint keeps it in a transmission control block (TCB): addresses and ports, the current state, sequence numbers, windows and timers.
example: TIME_WAIT keeps a stripped-down copy of the connection state so a repeated FIN can still be acknowledged.
